text: Gastrometrics turns your recipes into clear numbers: what each dish costs you, what to sell it for and how much it leaves you. This chapter shows you the big picture and the fastest path to your first result.

You enter your ingredients with what you pay for them, build your recipes with the quantities you use, and the app works out the real cost of every dish, suggests a selling price and shows your margin. From there, everything else —inventory, menus, purchasing, sales and reports— uses those same numbers, so you never have to type them twice.
Recipes are at the center: they read your ingredient prices and feed menus, purchase orders and reports. Change an ingredient's price and every recipe that uses it recalculates on its own.

Add 3 or 4 ingredients in Ingredients, with their purchase price and net content. You don't need your full inventory to get started. · Create your first recipe in the Recipe Sheet: pick those ingredients and enter the quantity you use of each. · See the result: production cost, suggested price and margin appear on the same screen, in real time. · Save and export the sheet as a PDF for your kitchen or your accountant. · Carry on whenever you like with inventory, menus or purchasing. They aren't required to see your first price. Rather see an example first?: If you don't have any recipes yet, the Dashboard offers “See an example first”: it creates a sample recipe with its cost and price already calculated so you can see how it works. You can delete it anytime.
Tip Shortcuts and good habits that save you time. ·  Important Details worth knowing before you press a button. ·  Plan Features that depend on your subscription plan (chapter 14).
Everything in Gastrometrics belongs to a business. Here you'll see how to sign up, create businesses, move between them and make the most of the Dashboard.

Sign-up is a 5-step wizard: your details and password, your professional information (country, currency, business type and size), the plan you want, acceptance of the terms, and a final summary. If you arrive from the pricing page with a plan already chosen, it comes preselected. Each plan shows what it includes and what it doesn't; Foodie (free) is selected by default. If you pick a paid plan, you go to the payment screen when you finish. The last step has an optional box to receive updates and reminders by email. It starts unchecked and you can change it anytime in Settings (chapter 15). When you sign in, the Remember me on this device box is checked: your session stays open. Uncheck it on a shared computer and the session ends when you close the browser. Didn’t get the confirmation email? Check your spam folder and, if it isn’t there, tap Resend the email on the “Check your email” screen or in the notice that appears when you try to log in without confirming. You can request it once a minute. Until you confirm your email you can’t enter the app.

Basics and logo. Name, description, business type and, if you like, a logo that will appear in the header of your PDFs. · Monthly fixed costs. Rent, utilities, staff, marketing and others. They're used to spread your fixed costs into the price of each dish (chapter 4). · Default pricing method. “Food Cost %” (recommended, selected by default) or “Gastrometrics” (6 cost items, advanced). Every new recipe inherits it, and you can change it recipe by recipe. Restaurant · Coffee shop · Bakery · Pastry shop · Food Truck · Catering · Bar · Pizzeria · Fast Food · Other Each business has its own ingredients, recipes, inventory, menus and purchasing: nothing mixes between businesses. Inside each business panel you can choose from 12 theme colors, which also color the accents of its PDFs.
Businesses shows one card per business with an “Open” button. While you work in any module, the side menu also lists your businesses so you can jump between them without going back to the start.

What to do today: ingredients below their minimum, recipes without a selling price and your average margin. Each card takes you straight to where you can fix it. · Key figures: total recipes, ingredients, businesses and average cost, across all your businesses. · Quick actions: one shortcut per module so you can jump in without the side menu. · Recent activity: what you and your team did (recipes, ingredients, imports, invitations). Notifications: what happened on its own or needs your attention: a price that went up after a cost change, a margin that went up, your plan changing or expiring, and support replies. Tap a notice to go handle it. While you get started, the Dashboard shows Your path: add ingredients, create your first recipe, reach 3 recipes and explore what's new. Each step takes you straight to where it's done. You can hide it with the X. The Your path buttons open the import directly: "Import my ingredients" and "Import a recipe". If you'd rather start from scratch, each step also has the manual option.

Dashboard — An overview of your whole account and what needs attention. · Recipe Sheet — Create or edit a recipe, with its cost and price. · My Recipes — Search, duplicate, move and recover recipes. · Ingredients — Your ingredient database, prices and waste. · Inventory — Stock, counts and minimum-level alerts. · Team — Invite people and give them permissions. · Menus — Build menus by course for service or events. · Purchase Orders — Supplier orders, by hand or suggested. · Sales — Record sales, import your POS and issue invoices. · Reports — Business overview and finances. · Businesses — Create, open and delete businesses. The menu fills in as you go: So you're not overwhelmed, the menu starts with the essentials. With your first recipe, Reports and Sales appear; with 3 recipes, Inventory, Menus, Purchase orders and Team, marked "New". To see everything from the start, use "Show all modules now" at the bottom of the menu. Tutorials and what's new: Each section has a guided tour that appears the first time you open it; replay it anytime with Restart tutorial in the menu. When we add something new, you'll see the What's new window with a See the tutorial button that takes you to that section and shows you what's new step by step. The update email has the same link. Nothing gets lost, and dates are day/month/year: If you close or leave without saving a new recipe, a new ingredien
Your ingredients are the foundation of all costing. If their prices are up to date, so are your recipes, menus and reports.

Name, category, unit of measure, supplier, purchase pack (optional) and its price: what you pay for the whole pack and how much it contains. From that the app calculates the price per unit, which is what your recipes actually use. Price per unit: Price per unit = Purchase price ÷ Net content. Net content is in the ingredient's base unit (grams, milliliters, units…). Purchase price of the sack 450.00 · Net content 25000 g · Price per gram 0.018 · A recipe using 300 g costs 300 × 0.018 = 5.40

Categories are a fixed list of 40 (Poultry, Beef, Fish, Dairy, Flour, Spices, Beverages, Spirits, Wine, Beer, Soft drinks & mixers, Disposables…), plus a special one, Sub-recipe / production, assigned automatically to preparations you use as an ingredient (chapter 5). The available units are: Grams · Kilograms · Milliliters · Liters · Ounces · Fluid ounces · Pounds · Gallons · Unit Use Unit for items you count (eggs, cans, bread rolls). The app treats them specially, for example to warn you if a recipe's yield looks too low. Don't forget packaging: Cups, takeout boxes, bags, napkins or straws are part of each dish's cost too. Add them as ingredients in the Disposables category (for example, a pack of 100 boxes, by unit) and put them in the recipe of what you sell to go. Otherwise your price won't cover them.
If you buy by the Box, Sack, Bottle, Can, Bag or Jar, save how much each pack contains. That way your purchase orders say “4 boxes” instead of a quantity in grams nobody would order.

Load your whole database at once from Excel, CSV or a pasted list, and export it to Excel whenever you want. If you'd rather start from a format, the app generates a template with its real categories and units; headers are recognized in all 6 languages. The guided Ingredients tour ends by opening this import, so you can load your whole list at once. If you prefer, you can also add them one by one with "New ingredient". You don't need the template: upload your file as it is (.xlsx, .xls or .csv) or paste your list copied from Excel, Google Sheets, an email or WhatsApp, one per line (for example "Tomato, 2 kg, 3.50"). The app recognizes columns even with other names or no titles, prices with currency symbols and a decimal comma or point ("$8,50", "1,250.75") and content written next to the unit ("25 kg bag"). If the list has no category, one is suggested from the name. You see everything before importing: The preview shows each ingredient with its content, price and status: "Ready", "No price" or "Already exists" (those are skipped). When it finishes, the app offers the next step: importing your recipes. Prices and currency: Prices are saved in your account's currency (Settings); the app does not convert between currencies. They're accepted with a symbol or code and with a decimal comma or point: "$8,50" and "8.50" are 8.50, "1.250,75" and "1,250.75" are 1250.75. A number like "1

Waste is what you pay for but can't use: peels, bones, trimmings, evaporation. In Manage Waste you switch the system on and, for each ingredient, choose the typical percentage for its category or your own (or a fixed amount). Real cost with waste: Usable content = Net content × (1 − waste %) ; Price per unit = Purchase price ÷ Usable content. You pay for all of it but only use part, so the real price per unit goes up. Turn waste off and everything returns to the original values. Some typical percentages by category: Seafood 63 %, Fish 52 %, Beef 33 %, Poultry 27 %, Fruit 24 %, Vegetables 21 %. Dry and packaged goods start at 0 %. Bar categories have their own typical waste: spirits 2 %, wine 5 %, draft beer 18 % and bottled beer 0 % (chapter 6). Plan: Waste management is available from the Home Cook plan.

In the last step of each ingredient you tick which of the 14 allergens that must be declared it contains (gluten, milk, eggs, tree nuts, soy, fish, crustaceans, sesame…). Recipes that use it —also through their sub-recipes— show them automatically in the Recipe Sheet, in the recipe's three PDFs and under each dish on the customer menu. They're never typed into the recipe by hand, so they don't go out of date.
Before you confirm, the app shows which recipes use it. It won't stop you, but you'll know which recipes will be left with a missing ingredient.
The heart of Gastrometrics: you turn a list of ingredients into an exact cost and a well-founded selling price, always seeing where each number comes from.

Name and Classification (22 options, from Hot line to Pastry or R&D). The “Sub-recipe” classification turns the recipe into an ingredient (chapter 5). The 5 “Bar · …” classifications calculate the price with pour cost (chapter 6). · Course: where it goes in service (starter, main, dessert…). · Yield: how much the recipe makes (8 portions, 1200 g…) with its unit. · Ingredients: search your database and enter the quantity. Each line shows what it costs. · Procedure and notes, plus a photo of the dish. Move on with Enter: In the first fields, pressing Enter takes you to the next one, so you can fill in the sheet almost without touching the mouse.

section: Your progress is saved for 24 hours
text: While you create a new recipe, Gastrometrics keeps an automatic draft. If you close the tab, lose your connection or go to another module, coming back to the Recipe Sheet brings the recipe back exactly as you left it, with a notice at the top. The draft lasts 24 hours from your last change and is also there if you sign in from another device. Want to start from scratch? Use Clear sheet (next to “Save Recipe” or in the notice). It asks for confirmation and erases everything: name, ingredients, procedure, photo, prices and the saved draft. Saving the recipe deletes the draft automatically.

Cost of each ingredient and of the recipe: Line cost = Quantity × Price per unit ; Production cost = Sum of all lines.  Unit cost: Unit cost = Production cost ÷ Yield. If you don't enter a yield, the app estimates it from the total weight of ingredients measured in g, ml, kg or liters.

section: Two ways to calculate the price
text: Each recipe uses one of two methods. New recipes start with Food Cost %; your business can change that default and you can switch recipe by recipe without losing anything: both start from the same real cost. Recipes you saved earlier with 6 cost items stay as they were. Method 1 Gastrometrics (6 cost items, advanced) Spreads your profit across six items, each a percentage of production cost: utilities 10 %, marketing 10 %, operating costs 30 %, labor 25 %, tax 0 % and net profit 30 % (all editable). · Method 2 Food Cost % (default) You choose what share of the price the ingredient cost should represent (usually 28 % to 35 %) and the price is worked out from there. It's the industry standard. Suggested selling price: 6 cost items: Price = Unit cost + (Sum of items ÷ Yield) ; Food Cost: Price = Unit cost ÷ Target % × (1 + Sales tax). In Food Cost, sales tax (if you use it) is added on top of the price and included in it; with 6 cost items it's one of the items. In both cases the price is rounded up to your currency's step: to 5 in lempiras (61 becomes 65, never 60), to 0.50 in dollars or euros (10.60 becomes 11.00), to 100 in colones. It's the only rounding in the calculation. The example below is in lempiras. 6 items: 2 + 2 + 6 + 5 + 0 + 6 21 · 20 + 21 = 41 → rounded 45 · Food Cost 30 %: 20 ÷ 0.30 = 66.67 → rounded 70 If your business has fixed costs and an estimate of dishes pe

If you sell through a delivery app or take card payments, enter in the recipe the commission % they keep from the price. The suggested price covers it, and the sheet shows the commission per unit and what you keep after paying it. Profit and margin already deduct it. Price with commission: Price = Price without commission ÷ (1 − Commission %). It works with both methods and is rounded afterwards, as always. Price without commission: 20 ÷ 0.30 66.67 · 66.67 ÷ (1 − 0.30) = 95.24 → rounded 100 · The app keeps 30 % 30 · You keep per dish 70

Recipe indicators: Total sales = Final price × Yield ; Contribution margin = (Total sales − Production cost) ÷ Total sales ; Cost % = Production cost ÷ Total sales.  The suggested price is never mandatory: you can type your own selling price or your own unit profit. Margins recalculate with your number, but cost always reflects what you really pay.

Enter how many people you want to serve and the app scales every quantity and cost instantly, always rounding up so you never fall short. It's a preview: the saved recipe doesn't change. Rounding is to the gram or milliliter in kg and L, and to 0.1 in g, ml, oz and units. Export PDF or Generate Purchase Order with PAX active uses the scaled quantities, without saving anything. The button warns you “Scaled to N”. · Saving with PAX active asks for confirmation: the recipe is stored at the new size and the previous size is kept as the “original”. · Restore original recipe goes back to that original size. Prices are updated to today's. Then press Save to confirm it. Suspicious yield: If any ingredient measured in “units” is 20 times the declared yield or more (for example, 200 eggs for a yield of 1), you'll see a yellow warning in the sheet and in the PDF. It doesn't block anything: it just helps you catch a typo.

In My Recipes, Import recipe turns a recipe you already have into a recipe sheet: paste it as you have it (from Word, WhatsApp or a website), upload a text file (.txt, .csv, .md), an Excel file (.xlsx, .xls) or a PDF, or take a photo with your phone camera. The app recognizes the name, servings, ingredients with quantity and unit (200 g, 2 cups, ½ kg, "to taste", tables, lists…) and the steps. You review it before it opens: Each ingredient is matched with your database and its quantity is converted to that ingredient's unit. Ones you don't have can be created (no price; you complete it later in Ingredients), picked from your list or skipped. Nothing is saved until you press Save in the Recipe Sheet. Recipe photos: The photo is read on your own phone or computer (it isn't uploaded to any server). You'll see the photo next to the text read, with the reading confidence and doubtful lines highlighted: tap them to fix them before continuing. For best results, shoot straight on, with good light and no shadows, and choose the language the recipe is written in. Recipe language: You don't have to choose it: the app assumes the recipe is in the language you use in the app and detects on its own if it's in another one (for example, an English or Chinese recipe), then reads it again with the right language. If you want to set it yourself, use "Change" next to the language; if you change it

section: My Recipes: duplicate, move and trash
text: Search by name, filter by classification and sort by name, cost, date or margin (margin is measured as on the Recipe Sheet; recipes without a price go last). Duplicate creates a copy in the same business, with “(copy)” in the name. · Migrate copies the recipe to another of your businesses. It asks whether to bring its ingredients and sub-recipes too (reusing those that already exist there) or just the recipe: in that case its sheet opens in the business so you pick the ingredients from its own database (those with the same name are linked automatically). · Delete sends it to the trash, where you can recover it for 30 days before it's removed automatically.
A base sauce, a stock or a dough you use in many dishes. You create it once and use it like any other ingredient.

Create the recipe as usual and give it the classification “Sub-recipe”. When you save it, Gastrometrics creates an ingredient with the same name that you can search for and add to any other recipe sheet. Cost of use: Cost of use = Total cost of the sub-recipe ÷ Yield. It's what each unit of the preparation costs (each gram of sauce, for example) when you use it in another recipe.

It usually isn't sold on its own, so its summary shows just three figures: production cost, yield and cost of use. If you also sell it separately, you can type a sale price by hand in “Unit sale price”.

If an ingredient in your base sauce goes up, its cost of use recalculates and the change reaches every dish that uses it automatically, at any level (including sub-recipes that use another sub-recipe). Those dishes follow the “price only goes up” rule. Saving the sub-recipe also instantly recalculates the recipes that use it. You don't need to open any recipe.

If you typed a sale price by hand on a sub-recipe and its cost goes up, the app asks whether you also want to raise that price to the suggested one: Yes, update all, Choose one by one or No, costs only. With “Remember my choice” it won't ask again for those sub-recipes. To change or uncheck it, open the sub-recipe and pick under “Sale price when the cost goes up”: Ask me every time, Always update or Never update. Watch the quantities: Cost of use is usually per gram or milliliter. If you type “150” thinking of units instead of grams, the dish's cost shoots up. Check the unit before saving.
Wine, beer, cocktails and non-alcoholic drinks are costed just like food: they're ingredients and recipes with a few bar adjustments. There's no separate module to learn.

Enter each bottle, can or keg as an ingredient, in milliliters or liters, with its price and content. There are bar categories of their own, each with its typical waste (spills, bottom of the bottle, foam): Spirits — 2 % — Shot 45 ml, double 90 ml, bottle · Wine — 5 % — Glass 150 or 125 ml, carafe 500 ml, bottle · Draft beer — 18 % — Pint 473 ml, half liter, glass 330 ml · Bottled beer — 0 % — Whole bottle or can · Soft drinks & mixers — 2 % — Whole container or glass 250 ml

A cocktail is a recipe with its lines in milliliters. When you pick a Bar · … classification, the price is calculated with pour cost: the share of the price that is product cost. That target belongs to that recipe only: it doesn't change your dishes' target. Bar · Cocktails — 20 % — 15–22 % · Bar · Wine — 30 % — 25–35 % · Bar · Beer — 24 % — 20–28 % · Bar · Non-alcoholic — 15 % — 10–20 % · Bar · Coffee & tea — 20 % — 15–25 % Price of a drink: Price = Cost per serving ÷ Target pour cost. It's rounded up to your currency's step, like any suggested price. Gin, 45 ml 1.69 · Tonic, 150 ml 0.55 · Lime 0.10 · Cost of the drink 2.34 · 2.34 ÷ 0.22 = 10.64 → rounded 11.00

section: Sell by the glass or bottle
text: In Ingredients, find the drink and tap the glass icon on its row. · Choose how it's served: a measure (glass, shot, pint…), another amount in milliliters or the whole container. · Check the cost per serving, how many servings each container gives and the suggested price; you can type your own price. · Tap Create recipe: it appears in My Recipes and can be used right away in menus, sales and theoretical stock. Cost per serving: Cost per serving = Milliliters served × Price per milliliter ; Servings per container = Usable content ÷ Milliliters served. The price per milliliter already includes the ingredient's waste. Selling the whole bottle costs exactly its purchase price. 750 ml bottle 20.00 · With 5 % waste you have 712.5 ml · Price per milliliter 0.028 · 150 ml glass 4.21 · Glasses per bottle 4.75

When you record inventory by pack you can use decimals (2.3 bottles). In the Inventory table, drinks show their stock, their minimum and the last count's difference in bottles too. Count by weight: Open fraction = (Weight − Empty) ÷ (Full − Empty) ; Containers = Unopened + Open fraction. Tap the scale icon when counting. You weigh an unopened full bottle and an empty one of the same product just once; they're saved for future counts. What the count tells you: In a bar, actual cost usually ends up several points above theoretical because of spills, over-pouring or comps. The count's difference, in bottles, tells you where to look first.

In Reports → Finance, the Kitchen vs. bar card shows each area's sales, share of sales and theoretical cost, plus the actual cost if you did an opening and a closing count in the period. Menu Engineering has an All / Kitchen / Bar filter to compare drinks with drinks and dishes with dishes. Plan: Bar recipes and “Sell by the glass”: all plans. Waste: from Home Cook. Inventory: from Chef de Partie. Kitchen vs. bar in Finance: from Sous Chef.
Know what you have, what's running out and what your storeroom is worth. Every count is kept as history.

Each item has a minimum you set yourself, right in the table. The app uses it to mark its status: Critical — Stock is equal to or below the minimum. · Low — Stock is equal to or below twice the minimum. · Normal — Stock is above twice the minimum, or it hasn't been counted yet.

“Register Inventory” saves a snapshot of your stock at that moment and updates current quantities. There are three types: Count Initial Inventory What you have at the start of a shift, week or month. · Count Final Inventory What's left at the end of the period, to compare with the initial count. · Stock in New Purchase Goods that just arrived, with the price you paid. Updates your recipe costs if the price changed. You can count in the base unit (grams, for example) or by pack (3 sacks), and the app does the conversion. When counting by pack you can use decimals: 2.3 bottles means 2 full ones and 3 tenths of the open one. The real content of the container is always counted, even if the ingredient has waste. Reading the count from a photo, PDF or Excel: In the ingredients step, "Photo of the count" or "Upload file (photo, PDF or Excel)" read your count sheet: each line with a name and a quantity ("Flour 25 kg", "Olive oil … 3") is matched with an ingredient in your database and its quantity fills in automatically, converted to the ingredient's unit (if the line has no unit, the ingredient's unit is used). Lines that don't match any ingredient are listed so you can enter them by hand. Check the quantities in the table before saving. Plan: Counting from a photo, PDF or Excel comes with Inventory (from Chef de Partie).

Inventory value: Item value = Stock × Container price ÷ Container content ; Total value = Sum of all items. Stock is stored in the ingredient's unit (ml, g…) and the price is for the whole bottle, sack or box: that's why it's divided by its content. Three 750 ml bottles at 20 are worth 60. With every new purchase the app also keeps a weighted average cost as a valuation reference. Recipe costing always uses the price of the latest purchase. Automatic recalculation: If a purchase changes an ingredient's price, every recipe and sub-recipe that uses it recalculates, and the app tells you how many. Prices only go up: If an ingredient's cost rises and a recipe's price falls short, the recipe moves up to the new suggested price. If the cost drops, the price does not drop: it stays as if you had typed it in «Unit selling price», and the app tells you in Notifications how much your margin rose. To lower it, change it yourself in the Recipe Sheet. For a sub-recipe with a hand-written sale price, the app asks you first (see Sub-recipes).

section: Theoretical stock: how much should be left
text: Besides the counted stock, each item shows its theoretical stock: what should be left based on the sales you recorded after the last count (manual, POS and invoices). Gastrometrics expands every sale through its recipe —including sub-recipes and waste— and deducts it automatically. Editing or deleting a sale corrects the number instantly. Theoretical stock: Theoretical stock = Last count + Purchases received − Sales consumption. A dish sold consumes one portion of its recipe; a menu sold, one portion of each active dish. When you do a new count, you'll see the last count difference: what you counted minus what the theory expected. If it's negative, more went out than your recipes explain (waste, waste, larger portions or missing stock): that's your cue to look into it.
Group your recipes into courses to build a menu, a daily special or an event, with its average price and purchase order.

Details: name, type (lunch, dinner, brunch, buffet, tasting, catering, special event or other), date and number of guests. · Courses: Starter, Main and Dessert by default. You can rename, remove or add more. · Dishes: the app suggests first the recipes whose “Course” matches each one. · Review: the full summary, with the option to set how many portions of each dish you need for that service. Drinks menu: Pick the Drinks menu type and the courses change to Cocktails, Wines, Beers and Non-alcoholic drinks. Each one suggests the recipes with the matching bar classification (chapter 6). Each dish can have its own price (otherwise it uses its recipe sheet price) and can be temporarily turned off without removing it from the menu. Menu average price: Average price = Sum of active dish prices ÷ Number of active dishes. Dishes that are turned off don't count.
From each menu you can export the PDF for your guests or the internal version with costs (chapter 12), or generate the purchase order with everything needed to produce it.

In the side menu, MEP (or the “View MEP (mise en place)” button on each menu) shows everything you need to make for a menu. By menu course, each dish is a heading with its checkbox and, below it, its sub-recipes as a checklist, with the amount that dish needs (and, further in, the sub-recipes of each sub-recipe). If a sub-recipe is also used in another dish, it tells you. Tap any of them to see its ingredients with scaled amounts, the procedure and a link to its sheet. At the end, Total per sub-recipe adds up all dishes, in case you make it at once. Portions: the ones you set for each dish in the menu; otherwise, the menu’s guest count. · Base preps: they come first because they’re made earlier; preps used by other preps appear above them. · Done: check each row when it’s ready; progress is remembered on that device and can be reset. How much to make: Multiplier = Menu portions ÷ Recipe yield ; Quantity = Quantity in the recipe × Multiplier. Each quantity is rounded up with the same rule as the Recipe Sheet’s PAX modifier, so you never come up short.

section: By menu course or by kitchen area
text: With “Group by” you choose to see the MEP by menu course (starter, main course…) or by kitchen area, which are the Recipe Sheet classifications (hot line, cold line, sauces and stocks, pastry, bar…). Tap an area to see only its items. One sheet per station: The Send button downloads, prints or sends by WhatsApp or email exactly what you’re viewing. The PDF starts with the list and checkboxes, then one recipe per page. Grouped by area, each area starts on a new sheet: print it and hand each station its own.
Tell each supplier exactly what and how much you need: by hand, from a menu or a recipe, or by letting the app suggest it from your inventory.

section: Four ways to create an order
text: By hand: search for each ingredient and the app fills in its unit, supplier and price. · Suggested from low stock: checks your inventory and builds the order with everything that's low or critical. · From a menu: everything needed to produce it, minus what you already have. · From a recipe: the “Generate Purchase Order” button in the Recipe Sheet, already scaled if you use the PAX modifier. Suggested quantity for low stock: Quantity to order = Larger of (2 × Minimum − Current stock) and the Minimum. It restocks up to twice your minimum to give you headroom, and never suggests less than the minimum itself. Order total: Line cost = Quantity × Price per unit ; Total = Sum of lines + Tax. Tax is 0 % by default and you can change it. If the ingredient has a pack, the order also tells you how many packs to buy, rounding up.

Pending · Approved · Ordered · Received · Cancelled You can change the status freely. Items are grouped by supplier (those without a supplier go last) so you can call each one with their full list. You can also duplicate or edit an order. “Received” adds to your inventory: When you mark an order as received, its quantities are added automatically to the stock of those items in inventory (matched by ingredient, even if you renamed it, or by name). If a product isn't in Inventory, the app tells you which. Sales tax, notes and the delivery date are kept when you edit the order. If what arrived differs from the order, correct it by recording the real amounts in Inventory → New Purchase.

Each order’s Send button shares it by WhatsApp (a message with the list; you pick the chat) or by email (the PDF downloads and your email opens so you choose who and attach it). On a phone, “Share PDF…” sends it with the PDF attached to the app you choose. The PDF button still downloads it as always. Plan: Manual orders are available from Home Cook; automatic suggestions from Chef de Partie.
Record what you sell to compare your prices with reality: by hand, by importing your point-of-sale (POS) system or by issuing invoices to your customers.

Manual entry: ideal if you don't have a POS. Pick a recipe or a menu and the quantity sold; the app calculates revenue and cost. · Import your POS: upload an .xlsx, .xls, .csv or .txt file. You tell it once which column is the dish, quantity, date and price, and save that as a named template. Next time, the app recognizes it on its own. Tricky files: The app detects whether your dates come as day/month or month/day (and lets you correct it), and reads accents and special characters correctly from older Windows-format files.

In the Invoices tab you create the invoice you hand to your customer: pick recipes or menus (or type lines by hand), with automatic numbering, editable tax, notes and your business logo on the PDF. Each invoice automatically counts as a sale in your reports (without tax). Not an official tax invoice: The Gastrometrics invoice doesn't include numbering authorized by any tax authority. Check your country's requirements before using it as a tax document.

At the bottom of the page, the history brings together all your sales (manual, POS and invoices), grouped by day, week, month or year, for the date range you choose, with a button to export it to PDF. Plan: Invoices: from Home Cook. Manual entry: from Chef de Partie. POS import: from Sous Chef.
This is where your numbers make sense: which recipes earn the most, what your inventory is worth and how your business is really doing.

General counts, inventory value and items on alert, average cost and margin, recipes by classification, most-used ingredients and the recipes with the best and worst margin. Cost % and margin are measured as on the Recipe Sheet: without the sales tax included in the price and after commission.

If you sell drinks, the Kitchen vs. bar card separates sales, theoretical cost and actual cost for each area (chapter 6). Profit and loss statement (P&L), your theoretical versus real food cost based on your sales, price changes by supplier, and Menu Engineering, which classifies each dish with Kasavana and Smith's standard method: it's popular if it sells at least 70% of its even share, and its margin is high if its margin per plate (price − cost) beats the average margin per plate sold. Cost percentages, Prime Cost and the P&L are measured on net sales, without the sales tax included in prices (same as the recipe sheet): Star — High — High — Protect it and feature it on your menu. · Cash cow — High — Low — It sells well: review its cost or raise its price a little. · Puzzle — Low — High — Good margin: promote it or improve its presentation. · Dog — Low — Low — Consider redesigning it or taking it off the menu. Cost of goods sold (COGS): COGS = Opening inventory + Purchases − Closing inventory. For an exact figure you need an opening and a closing count in the period.

Each ingredient’s price history and which supplier you bought it from, with a table comparing your suppliers (last price, lowest, number of purchases). It shows where you could save (another supplier sold it to you cheaper, with the estimated monthly saving), what went up the most in 30 days and a summary of each supplier. Prices come from your purchase orders (excluding cancelled), Inventory purchases, price changes and each ingredient’s current price.

Information based on the waste you set in Ingredients (chapter 3), either its category’s global value or a custom one: how much of what you buy is usable, how much more each unit costs, how much you lose on each purchase and an estimated monthly cost based on what you bought in the last 90 days. It also suggests ingredients without waste turned on whose category usually loses quite a bit. Plan: Overview: from Chef de Partie. Finance: from Sous Chef.
Each document is designed for whoever will read it: your kitchen, your management, your supplier or your customer. Costs never mix with documents meant for outsiders.

Recipe sheet · Administrative — Owner and management — Ingredients with costs, cost items, charts, margin and food cost. · Recipe sheet · Kitchen — Your kitchen team — Ingredients, quantities, photo and procedure, with no money figures. · Recipe sheet · Quick — Suppliers or partners — The essentials of the recipe, without costs or prices. · Inventory — Management — Total value, value by category, top items and statuses. · Menu · Guest — Your diners — An elegant menu, with no cost figures. · Menu · Internal — Owner — Cost, price and margin per dish, with charts. · MEP · Mise en place — Each kitchen station — What to make and how much, with checkboxes, and one scaled recipe per page; by area, one sheet per station. · Purchase order — Suppliers — Ingredients by supplier, quantities and total. · Invoice — Your customer — Your logo, customer details, lines, tax and total. Recipe sheets and the customer menu include each dish's allergens, calculated from its ingredients at the moment you export (chapter 3). Automatic warnings: The administrative sheet warns you at the top if cost exceeds the selling price or if the yield looks mistyped, before you print an odd number. PDFs come out in the language selected in the app, use your currency and carry your business's logo and theme color. Plan: The kitchen sheet is included in every plan. The administrative sheet, from Home Cook.
Invite your team to work with you in Gastrometrics, each person with access only to what they need.

In Team you enter the person's email. They receive an invitation and create their own account; your subscription covers their access. With Sous Chef you can add 1 person and with Chef Ejecutivo up to 4 (each plan's users include you). There are no fixed roles: you set three things separately for each person. Scope — All your businesses, or just one. · Tools — Independent boxes: recipes, ingredients, waste, manual and automatic orders, inventory, menus, reports, sales, finance and managing the team. · PDF — None, kitchen (no costs) or administrative (with costs). Preview: Turn on preview to see the app exactly as that person would, with the same permissions. Permissions are truly enforced, not just on screen: someone without access to a tool can't see or save that data. If something is locked, the app explains whether it's because of the account's plan or because the owner restricted it.

Start for free and move up when you need to. Your data is never lost when you change plans. Foodie — Free — 1 — 1 — Recipes, ingredients, import from wherever your data already is (text, Excel, PDF, photos and receipts) and kitchen recipe sheet PDF (included in every plan). · Home Cook — $15 / month — 1 — 1 — Waste, manual purchase orders, administrative sheet, invoices and price updates from receipts or lists. · Chef de Partie — $35 / month — 1 — 1 — Inventory (with counts from a photo, PDF or Excel), menus, suggested orders, Reports · Overview and manual sales entry. · Sous Chef — $70 / month — 2 — 2 — Reports · Finance, P&L, Menu Engineering, POS import and Team (you + 1 person). · Chef Ejecutivo — $120 / month — 5 — 5 — Team of up to 4 people besides you. Available for businesses on request. If your plan has an end date (for example, the founding kitchen month), the sidebar shows how many days are left under your plan. Three days before and on the day itself we remind you in the app: you can pick the plan you want to keep and schedule the payment, which is charged the day your plan ends. Your plan only changes once Stripe confirms the payment; otherwise your account switches to Foodie and you keep all your data. Importing is free: Importing your recipes and ingredients from text, Excel, PDF (with text or scanned), photos or receipts is included in every plan, Foodie too, wi

Payments are processed by Stripe. From My Plan you can change plans or open the billing portal to update your card or cancel. Changes show up in your account automatically and you get a confirmation email. Whenever your plan changes —because you changed it, because the Gastrometrics team adjusted it, or because an assigned plan expired— we let you know by email and with a window when you open the Dashboard, listing exactly what you gain, what you lose and what your plan includes now. If you lose access to a section, your data isn't deleted: it becomes available again if you upgrade later. The change also shows up under Notifications on the Dashboard and, when you close the window, a short tour of your new plan starts: it points to each menu module with something new. If a module isn't visible yet because you need more recipes (chapter 2), the tour tells you how many you need instead of pointing to something hidden. If you cancel, you keep full access until the end of the period you've already paid for. My Plan shows you the exact date. When something is locked: You'll see a padlock and a button to My Plan. If you use the app as part of a team, the message tells you it's the account owner who controls that access.

chapter: Invite: give a month, get a month
section: Invite: give a month, get a month
text: Invite another chef or kitchen to Gastrometrics. Your colleague tries it free and you earn a month when they really get started.

chapter: Invite: give a month, get a month
text: Open My Plan: "Give a month, get a month" is right below your plan. The Invite shortcut in the side menu takes you straight there. · Copy your link or send it with the WhatsApp or email buttons. · Your colleague signs up with that link: they see a note with your name and get 30 days of Chef Ejecutivo, no card.

chapter: Invite: give a month, get a month
text: Your colleague — 30 days of Chef Ejecutivo free, no card, no commitment. When it ends they go back to Foodie on their own, with no charge; if they want to continue, they pick a plan. · You — A month when your colleague really gets started within their first 30 days: saves a recipe with cost or picks a paid plan. Up to 12 months a year. Your reward is Chef Ejecutivo, the most complete plan, and it never lowers your plan. On Foodie it starts today. If you already have a plan with an end date —for example, the founding-kitchen month— 30 days are added at the end and, if your plan was lower, you move up to Chef Ejecutivo. If you pay for your plan, you get one month of your plan as credit on your next invoice. Reminders: If your colleague hasn't started, we email you on day 3 and day 14. In Invite you see how many days they have left and can remind them on WhatsApp with one tap. The rules, always at hand: Tap the ? next to the Invite title to see all the rules. If they don't get started within 30 days, the invitation expires. Only new accounts of real people count. The program rules are also in the Terms of Use, section 4.7, and the Privacy Policy explains what the person who invited you sees: only your first name, sign-up date and invitation status, never your recipes or data.
Make the app your own, choose your language and currency, decide which emails you get and manage your account data.

Profile: name, email (changing it asks for your current password), country and business type. · Appearance: light, dark or follow your system. · Regional: country, currency and language. · Notifications: whether you want product updates and reminders by email. · Account: data backup, legal documents, delete content and delete the account.

The app is available in Spanish, English, Danish, French, Portuguese and Chinese. The language you choose is used across the interface, in your PDFs and in every email we send you. There are 21 currencies; changing currency changes the symbol and format, it doesn't convert your amounts. Decimals always use a point.

You always get your account emails: confirmation, password, payments and team invitations. If you turn on Updates and reminders, we'll also write when there are new features and, if you haven't signed in for a few days, a helpful reminder based on what you did last: Reminder Unfinished recipe Your Recipe Sheet draft is waiting for you before the 24 hours are up. · Reminder Inventory and reports When a week has passed since your last count or since you checked your reports. · Reminder Prices and coming back If your prices haven't been updated in over 30 days, or if you haven't visited in a while. And when your account has something specific to tell you, we email you the figure: Every Monday Weekly summary Your key numbers: average food cost, inventory value, items below minimum and dishes with low margin. · Alert Low stock and margin If an item reaches its minimum or a dish stops meeting its food cost target. · Team Invitations and businesses If your invitee hasn't joined, or a new business still has no recipes. · Milestones Progress and your plan When you reach 10, 25 or 50 recipes, and if your plan includes something you haven't tried yet. We never send more than one reminder every few days. Every email has a link to unsubscribe in one click, or you can uncheck the box in Settings → Notifications.

Download backup: a single file with all your content (recipes, ingredients, menus and more). · Delete all content: empties your account but keeps it active. You type your email to confirm. · Delete account: cancels your subscription and erases everything permanently. It also asks for your email to confirm. No going back: Deleting content or the account can't be undone. Download your backup first.

The most common “this isn't doing what I expected” situations, with their cause and fix. A recipe's cost comes out huge or absurd. — Check the yield and each ingredient's unit. If you use sub-recipes, make sure the quantity is in grams or milliliters, not units. · I changed a price and my recipes didn't move. — Recalculation is immediate. Make sure the recipe uses exactly that ingredient and not a duplicate with a similar name. · I can't see a module (Inventory, Finance, Team…). — Your plan doesn't include it, or the account owner didn't give you access. The on-screen message tells you which. · I marked an order as “Received” and an item wasn't added. — The app tells you which products weren't added: they don't exist in Inventory. Add them in Inventory and record the purchase in Inventory → New Purchase. · I saved a recipe with PAX active by mistake. — Use “Restore original recipe” and save again. · I left the Recipe Sheet without saving. — Go back to the Recipe Sheet within 24 hours: your recipe comes back on its own. · My emails arrive in another language. — Change the language in Settings → Regional while signed in; the next emails will arrive in that language. · I don't want reminders. — Use the “Stop receiving these emails” link or uncheck the box in Settings → Notifications. · My drink comes out with a very high price. — Check that its classification is a “Bar” one: that

On every screen of the app, bottom right (above the bottom bar on a phone), there is the help button. It never opens by itself or interrupts you: it only shows a number when you have an unread reply. Pick the topic of your question: Recipe Sheet, Ingredients, Inventory, Menus, Purchase orders, Sales and reports, Plans and billing, Account and team, Something isn’t working, An idea or Something else. · Type your question. As you type, the assistant shows the parts of this manual that answer it; tap them to read, or download the full manual as a PDF. · If that’s not enough, send it to the team. You can attach up to 3 files (3 MB in total): photos, PDF, Excel, CSV or text (the same formats the app accepts when importing). · Wait for your turn. We reply in order of arrival: the chat tells you how many people are ahead of you, or that you’re next. · Get the reply in the chat and by email, in your language. If you write again, you stay in the same conversation; once it’s solved, tap “It’s solved”. Send a ticket. The second tab of the help panel works like “Suggestions and reports”: pick the type (bug report, suggestion, complaint or your experience), write your message and, if you want, attach a screenshot. When you send it you see your ticket number, and we reply by email. You can also write to us from Suggestions and reports, at the bottom of Settings. We read every message.
